opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a good question, because the change has been dramatic, and I feel it in my day-to-day work.

When I started in this field, a research project was a few people, a handful of GPUs, and a dataset that fit on one machine. You had an idea, trained a model for a few days, and if the images looked a bit better than last year's, you wrote a paper. A lot of the early generative work was like that, including GANs and image-to-image translation. It was exploratory. The question was simply whether something was possible at all.

Now the question has shifted from "can we do it?" to "can we make it reliable and useful enough for someone to build on?" That changes the scale of everything. The models are much bigger, and the data pipelines are often harder engineering than the models themselves. Curating, filtering, and annotating huge amounts of video takes enormous effort. Training runs use thousands of GPUs for weeks, so you can't afford to be careless. One mistake in the data or the setup is very expensive.

The teams have changed too. It's no longer a few researchers. You need infrastructure people, data people, people who think about evaluation, and people who think about safety and how the model will actually be used. In some ways it feels more like building a product, or even a large scientific instrument, than writing a paper.

For me personally, the biggest shift is that the audience has changed. With work like world foundation models for physical AI, the users are developers building robots or autonomous vehicles. They don't care whether we beat a benchmark by half a point. They care whether the model understands physics well enough to generate useful training data or simulate scenarios they can trust. That pushes us to think much more about consistency, controllability, and how the model behaves in the long tail of cases.

I still think exploration matters a lot, though. The deployment phase is exciting, but many of the most important ideas came from small, curious experiments. So part of my job now is keeping a balance: building at scale, while protecting some room for the weird ideas that might matter five years from now.

r001.rationale: The response describes early AI research as small-scale and exploratory, and says exploration still matters. It does not express nostalgia for that period or say workable approaches had yet to be discovered.

fable-5.1.text:
Ming-Yu Liu: It's changed enormously, and honestly in ways I didn't fully anticipate when I started. Early on, when I was doing generative modeling research, the scale was almost intimate. You'd have a small team, maybe a handful of GPUs, and you could hold the entire problem in your head. You'd try an idea in the morning and know by evening whether it worked. The feedback loop was tight, and most of the work was really about intuition and taste, figuring out what the right question was.

Now, with something like Cosmos and world foundation models, the unit of work is completely different. We're not talking about a few GPUs, we're talking about thousands, and the datasets are measured in tens of millions of hours of video. A single training run is a serious commitment of resources, so you can't just try things casually anymore. Every experiment has to be justified. That changes how you think. You spend a lot more time on infrastructure, on data curation, on making sure the pipeline is reliable, because a bug that costs you a week at this scale is enormously expensive.

The other big shift is who you're building for. In the exploration phase, your audience is other researchers, and success is a paper that advances understanding. In deployment, your audience is people building robots, autonomous vehicles, factories. They have very concrete problems. A roboticist doesn't care that your model is elegant, they care whether it helps their arm pick up an object reliably. So the definition of progress moves from "is this interesting" to "is this useful," and those are not always the same thing.

And then there's the organizational scale. I went from working mostly with a few close collaborators to coordinating across many teams, with people who specialize in systems, in data, in evaluation, in safety. My role has become much more about setting direction and creating the conditions for others to do great work, rather than doing every piece myself. That was an adjustment. I think a lot of researchers struggle with it, because the thing that made you good at research, going deep on one problem, is not the thing that makes you good at leading a large effort.

But I'd say what hasn't changed is that the core still comes down to a few genuinely good ideas. All the scale in the world doesn't help if the fundamental approach is wrong. So I try to protect some portion of my time to still think like an explorer, even while most of the machine around me is focused on deployment. The challenge is keeping both of those alive at once.

r001.rationale: The response describes early research as intimate and exploratory, but it does not express nostalgia or say that workable approaches had yet to be discovered.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that the scope of the problem has expanded. When you’re exploring an idea, you can focus on a particular capability: Can we make this work? What happens if we try a different approach? As you move toward deployment, that capability becomes one part of a much larger system. You have to think about reliability, efficiency, and how people actually use it.

That also changes the way you work. Progress depends on more people working closely together, and on feedback from real use. Research still matters enormously, but the questions become broader. You’re asking both whether something is possible and what it takes to make it useful consistently. To me, that’s an exciting expansion of the work.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes how deployment broadens the work and calls that expansion exciting. It does not express nostalgia for an early period when workable approaches had yet to be discovered.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that the unit of work has expanded. In exploration, you can focus on a particular idea: can we make this model work, can we demonstrate a new capability? As you move toward deployment, the model becomes one part of a much larger system. Reliability, efficiency, and how people actually use it become central questions.

That changes how you think about research, too. A promising result is a starting point. You have to understand where it fails, what it costs to run, and whether the improvement translates into something useful for the user. So the work becomes more collaborative, and the feedback from real use becomes much more important.
